what: Colossus Mark 1, a programmable (plugs and switches) electronic valve machine, performed satisfactorily at Dollis Hill (GPO research station, London) under Tommy Flowers.

sources.title: Colossus computer
sources.quote: It performed satisfactorily at Dollis Hill on 8 December 1943

sources.title: Colossus computer
sources.quote: Colossus is regarded as the world's first programmable, electronic, digital computer.

note: Earlier candidates: Atanasoff-Berry computer (tested 1942) is electronic but not programmable; Zuse Z3 (May 1941) is programmable but electromechanical relays. Later and stricter readings: ENIAC (general-purpose, Dec 1945 / dedicated Feb 1946) and Manchester Baby (first stored-program, 21 June 1948). Colossus is not stored-program and was special-purpose, so fit to 'stores data and runs programs' is partial. The first pass (ENIAC 1945) was later.

what: Colossus Mark 1, installed at Bletchley Park, attacked its first Lorenz-cipher message (processing intercepted traffic for the Allies).

sources.title: Colossus computer
sources.quote: It was operational in January and it successfully attacked its first message on 5 February 1944.

note: Delivered to Bletchley 18 Jan 1944 and operational that month; first real message 5 Feb 1944. Rejected as earlier: ABC (never used for real work). ENIAC's first real program (Dec 1945) is later.
check_note: Checked for earlier candidates; none found that fits the definition and kind with a verifiable source. Original note: Delivered to Bletchley 18 Jan 1944 and operational that month; first real message 5 Feb 1944. Rejected as earlier: ABC (never used for real work). ENIAC's first real program (Dec 1945) is later.

what: Sir William Thomson's tide-predicting machine (built 1872-73 by Alexander Legé, with Edward Roberts); a model was exhibited at the British Association meeting, 1873.

sources.title: Tide-predicting machine
sources.quote: A model of it was exhibited at the British Association meeting in 1873

note: Judged on mechanism: continuous mechanical quantities (pulleys and cranks) summing harmonic terms, i.e. it models an equation, but it evaluates a fixed formula rather than solving general equations. If the definition is read strictly as 'solves differential equations', the earliest working machine is Bush's MIT differential analyzer (1928-31, first pass), with Hartree's Manchester model 1934. James Thomson's 1876 integrating machine was a description, not a working solver. Rejected as loose analogues: planimeters, astrolabe and the Antikythera mechanism (c.150-100 BC, an orrery, not an equation solver).

what: A larger tide-predicting machine (20 components) was built for the Government of India and used to generate tide data for Indian ports.

sources.title: Tide-predicting machine
sources.quote: An enlarged and improved version of the machine, for computing 20 tidal components, was built for the Government of India in 1879

note: The 1876 ten-component machine may have produced earlier tide tables but no use date was found. Arthur Pollen's naval fire-control analog computer (c.1912) and Bush's differential analyzer (1931, used operationally in the 1930s) are later.

what: Herman Hollerith's first tabulators compiled mortality statistics for Baltimore, Jersey City and New York City (trial of the card-and-counter system).

sources.title: Tabulating machine
sources.quote: Hollerith's first tabulators were used to compile mortality statistics for Baltimore, Jersey City and New York City in 1886.

note: Wikipedia says 1886; other histories (Smithsonian, Franklin Institute, USPTO, per search summaries I could not fetch) put the Baltimore trial in 1887, so the date may be 1887. Hollerith's patent application was filed 1884 but described a concept. Earlier punched-card machines (Jacquard 1804, Korsakov 1832 proposal) do not tabulate, count or sort records, so were rejected.

what: Hollerith electric tabulators compiled the 1890 US Census from about 100 million punched cards.

sources.title: Tabulating machine
sources.quote: Hollerith's method was used for the 1890 census.

note: The 1886/87 Baltimore mortality work was a trial; the 1890 census was the first large-scale official deployment. If the mortality compilation is counted as real use, the date would be 1886-87.

what: The Banu Musa brothers in Baghdad described an automatic flute player driven by a pinned barrel, in their Book of Ingenious Devices (c. 850).

sources.title: Banu Musa
sources.quote: credited with inventing the first music sequencer, as described in the manuscript, as an example of an early type of programmable machine.

sources.title: Banu Musa
sources.quote: a Persian family of polymaths, astronomers, mathematicians, and engineers active in 9th century Baghdad

note: Date is approximate (the book is conventionally dated c. 850; the page says only 9th century). Pinned-barrel machine plays a recorded sequence without an operator, so mechanism fits, though the page hedges ('may have been the first programmable machine'). Earlier: Hellenistic automata (e.g. Hero) not checked. The first pass (1952 MIT numerical control) and Jacquard 1804 are later.

what: Basile Bouchon, a silk-weaving worker in Lyon, controlled a drawloom with a perforated paper roll.

sources.title: Basile Bouchon
sources.quote: invented a way to control a loom with a perforated paper roll in 1725

sources.title: Basile Bouchon
sources.quote: This development is considered to be the first industrial application of a semi-automated machine.

note: Bouchon's loom still needed an extra operator, so it is only partly 'rather than by an operator'. Falcon 1728, Vaucanson 1745 and Jacquard (patent 1804, 'wildly successful' 1805) refined it; Jacquard is the first fully card-driven loom in wide use. Musical automata with pinned barrels (c. 850 on) were pleasure devices, not production use.

what: Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments demonstrated the first working integrated circuit (germanium, wire-bonded).

sources.title: Integrated circuit
sources.quote: successfully demonstrating the first working example of an integrated circuit on 12 September 1958

sources.title: Q80831
sources.quote: time of discovery or invention (P575): 1958

note: Earlier ideas considered: Jacobi's 1949 patent and Dummer's 1952 concept (concepts, no working circuit found); micromodules (1957) were assembled discrete parts. Noyce's monolithic planar IC followed about six months later.

what: Integrated circuits entered use in products and in the US space and military programs; NASA's Apollo program was the largest single consumer 1961-65.

sources.title: Integrated circuit
sources.quote: NASA's Apollo Program was the largest single consumer of integrated circuits between 1961 and 1965.

note: Date is inferred from the start of the 1961-65 consumption window; I did not confirm the first commercial IC sale (Texas Instruments/Fairchild, c. 1960-61), which may be slightly earlier. No earlier use of Kilby's 1958 prototype found.

what: General Electric built a demonstration computer from thin-film cryotrons (arrays of 2000 devices operated), following John Bremer's 1957 planar cryotron.

sources.title: Cryotron
sources.quote: In the next few years, a demonstration computer was made and arrays with 2000 devices operated.

note: The page gives only 'the next few years' after 1957, so the year 1960 is approximate (1958-1961). Buck's 1953-55 cryotron was a single switching element, not a computer. No machine described as a working superconducting computer was found in other sources. No practical use: cryotron work was abandoned by the mid-1960s and, per Wikipedia, there are no commercial superconducting computers as of 2016. No mass adoption.

what: Valdemar Poulsen invented the Telegraphone, the first magnetic recorder (steel wire); he demonstrated it at the 1900 Paris Exposition.

sources.title: Wire recording
sources.quote: The first crude magnetic recorder was invented in 1898 by Valdemar Poulsen.

note: Earlier: Oberlin Smith's 1888 Electrical World article proposed wire recording but no working machine is recorded. The definition includes sound, so the audio telegraphone counts. Later: tape 1928 (Pfleumer), drum 1932 (Tauschek), RAMAC disk 1956 (first pass).

what: The American Telegraphone Company of Springfield, Massachusetts manufactured the Telegraphone, the first commercially available magnetic recorder, for dictation and telephone recording.

sources.title: Wire recording
sources.quote: manufactured by the American Telegraphone Company, Springfield, Massachusetts in 1903

note: Page says use was 'extremely limited' through the 1920s-30s. Earlier practical use (e.g. the 1900 Paris demonstration recording of Franz Josef) was a demonstration. Digital data use began later with UNIVAC I tape (1951) and RAMAC (1956). mass_adoption left out: the page says affordable tape recorders for home and office appeared in the first half of the 1950s but gives no firm year.

what: John Benjamin Dancer produced microphotographs (daguerreotype images reduced 160:1), viewed through a microscope.

sources.title: Microphotography
sources.quote: John Benjamin Dancer was one of the first to produce microphotographs, in 1839.

note: Dancer's work was a novelty with no document-storage purpose; the idea of microphotography for preserving documents was first suggested by Glaisher in 1851 and Herschel in 1853. Fit to 'books and records on film read through a viewer' is loose, as the first pass said. Rene Dagron's 1859 patent and Otlet's 1906 microphotographic book are later.

what: During the Siege of Paris, Rene Dagron microphotographed dispatches on thin collodion film; carried by pigeon, they were projected by magic lantern and transcribed.

sources.title: Microform
sources.quote: By 28 January 1871, when Paris and the Government of National Defense surrendered, Dagron had delivered 115,000 messages to Paris by carrier pigeon.

note: Earlier than the first pass (Recordak 1928, bank cheques; page says commercial use began in the 1920s with McCarthy's 1925 Checkograph). The pigeon-post films carried messages and newspaper pages, a close match to records on film read through a projector.

what: Marvin Minsky and Dean Edmonds built SNARC (40 vacuum-tube neurons, Navy-funded) at Princeton; it learned to solve a maze.

sources.title: SNARC
sources.quote: They tested the machine on a copy of Shannon's maze, and found that it could learn to solve the maze.

sources.title: Marvin Minsky
sources.quote: In 1951, Minsky built SNARC, which is often considered the first artificial neural network.

note: Earlier than the first pass (Rosenblatt's perceptron 1957-58). McCulloch and Pitts (1943) was a non-learning mathematical model, not a built machine; Farley and Clark (1954) simulated a Hebbian network on a computer, later than SNARC. Exact month of SNARC working not found (funded summer 1951).

what: Bell Labs applied convolutional neural networks trained by backpropagation (LeNet) to handwritten digit recognition for zip codes, later reading cheques in ATMs.

sources.title: LeNet
sources.quote: In 1989, Yann LeCun et al. at Bell Labs first applied the backpropagation algorithm to practical applications

note: Widrow and Hoff's ADALINE (1960) and MADALINE (largest built 1963) adaptive filters are described by Wikipedia as 'likely the first artificial neural network applied to a real-world problem' (phone-line echo removal), which would be earlier, but I found no dated first deployment. The CIA studied the Mark I Perceptron 1960-64 only as an evaluation.

what: John Blankenbaker designed the Kenbak-1, a TTL-logic 8-bit computer intended for individuals and schools.

sources.title: Kenbak-1
sources.quote: Designed in 1970 by John Blankenbaker

what: IBM presented the Naval Ordnance Research Calculator (NORC) to the US Navy; at the ceremony it calculated pi to 3,089 digits in 13 minutes.

sources.title: IBM NORC
sources.quote: At the presentation ceremony, it calculated pi to 3,089 digits, which was a record at the time.

note: NORC was 'likely the most powerful computer at the time' but is not usually called a supercomputer, so fit is uncertain. Later contenders: UNIVAC LARC (delivered June 1960), IBM 7030 Stretch (1961), Atlas (1962), CDC 6600 (1964, first pass 1965).

what: NORC moved to the Naval Proving Ground at Dahlgren, Virginia and was the main computer there (ballistics and ordnance calculations) until 1958.

sources.title: IBM NORC
sources.quote: In 1955, NORC was moved to the Naval Proving Ground at Dahlgren, Virginia. It was their main computer until 1958

note: It went into service December 1954 at the Watson laboratory; 1955 Dahlgren is the clear working deployment. LARC delivery to Livermore (June 1960) is later.

what: ENIAC was used for calculations of thermonuclear reactions for Los Alamos, its first program.

sources.title: ENIAC
sources.quote: In December 1945, the ENIAC was used to calculate thermonuclear reactions.

sources.title: Computer simulation
sources.quote: its first large-scale deployment during the Manhattan Project in World War II to model the process of nuclear detonation

note: Earlier than the first pass (ENIAC Monte Carlo, spring 1948, 'first fully automated Monte Carlo calculations'). Wikipedia dates the first large-scale computer simulation to the Manhattan Project (1944-45, by punched-card machines) but I did not confirm a date or a computer. Whether the Dec 1945 run counts as a model simulation rather than a calculation is a judgment; the 1944 Cambridge differential-analyzer simulations of transmission lines are not a first.

what: The same ENIAC run served Los Alamos hydrogen-bomb feasibility research.

sources.title: ENIAC
sources.quote: its first program was a study of the feasibility of the thermonuclear weapon

note: Same event as first_demonstration. Monte Carlo neutron-diffusion simulations followed in spring 1948 (Von Neumann, Metropolis).

what: GM Research's 'Digital Design' (later DAC-1) interactive graphics design system shown working at General Motors, 1959

sources.title: DAC-1
sources.quote: The system, known as Digital Design, was demonstrated and improved throughout 1959.

note: Rejected later candidates: DAC-1 full demo at IBM Kingston Dec 1962, Sketchpad (Sutherland, Jan 1963 report), DAC-1 public unveiling 1964; Hanratty's PRONTO (1957) is numerical-control programming, not interactive design by computer. The 1959 date rests on one Wikipedia statement and the early system's scope is unclear.

what: Production DAC-1 went live at GM in Warren, Michigan, used to design automobile parts (trunk lid modelled Nov 1963)

sources.title: DAC-1
sources.quote: The production DAC-1 system went live in Warren in April 1963.

note: Sketchpad (1963) was a thesis research system, not production. Earlier numerical-control tools (PRONTO 1957) are machining aids and were not counted. Not exhaustive for other countries (e.g. Citroen SPAC, Renault, 1960s).

what: Test at Bedford, Massachusetts: radar data sent over telephone lines to a computer (Whirlwind), showing detection of a mock enemy aircraft; directed by C. Robert Wieser

sources.title: Semi-Automatic Ground Environment
sources.quote: data produced by a radar was transmitted through telephone lines to a computer for the first time, showing the detection of a mock enemy aircraft.

note: Earlier candidates: wartime radar/teleprinter links and Bell Labs relay computers remote-operated by teletype (1940 Complex Number Calculator demo, not checked here). Later: SAGE network 1958, SABRE 1960, CTSS 1961, ARPANET 1969. Chose 1951 test as first computer reached over lines from a distant sensor; not exhaustive.

what: SAGE New York sector became operational: computers linked by telephone/modem lines to radar sites and other centers in routine air defense

sources.title: Semi-Automatic Ground Environment
sources.quote: On "June 26, 1958,…the New York sector became operational"

note: Later: SABRE airline reservations 1960 (Wikipedia Computer network: 'In 1960, the commercial airline reservation system semi-automatic business research environment (SABRE) went online'), CTSS remote users. Pre-SAGE operational use (e.g. Cape Cod System tests from 1953, manual-era links) were tests, not service.

what: First ARPANET message UCLA to SRI (Wikidata inception of the Internet)
note: Only fits the network part of the definition (not worldwide, not for ordinary people). sources.title: Internet

note: Year is a judgement; the source supports 1995 as a turning point, not a user count. Adoption by ordinary households was later (2000s) in many countries.

what: First ARPANET network mail sent (Ray Tomlinson, BBN), introducing user@host addressing

sources.title: Email

what: Lockheed completed the earliest form of Dialog under Roger K. Summit, an online interactive retrieval system

sources.title: Dialog (online database)
sources.quote: The earliest form of the Dialog system was completed in 1966 in Lockheed under the direction of Roger K. Summit.

note: Earlier candidate: MEDLARS (NLM, 1964), a batch computer retrieval service, not interactive 'in seconds'; also pre-computer mechanical retrieval (Goldberg's Statistical Machine, 1931) rejected as not computerized.

what: Lockheed's interactive Dialog system (Roger Summit) was tested on NASA's STAR database at Ames in 1966, cutting searches from 14 hours to a few minutes; this became NASA RECON.

sources.title: Roger K. Summit
sources.quote: Information searches within the NASA STAR database went from taking 14 hours, plus shipping and handling, to a few minutes with Summit's Dialog system.

sources.title: Dialog (online database)
sources.quote: The earliest form of the Dialog system was completed in 1966 in Lockheed under the direction of Roger K. Summit.

note: Replaces MEDLINE late 1971: Dialog was online and interactive on a large NASA database in 1966 (Ames experiment, NASA contract 1966). Result time is 'a few minutes' not strictly seconds, and 1966 was an experiment before RECON (1967 award); MEDLARS 1964 was batch. Original note: Rejected earlier: MEDLARS 1964 (launched by NLM, 'first large-scale, computer-based, retrospective search service available to the general public') was a real service but batch-mode, so it does not meet 'in seconds'. Dialog commercial service started ~1972 (not sourced). If batch counts, practical use is 1964.

what: MIT's START natural-language system went online on the Internet in 1993 and answered English questions on many topics (Boris Katz, MIT)

sources.title: Boris Katz
sources.quote: Boris Katz is the creator of the START information processing system (since 1993 - on the Internet)

sources.title: Boris Katz
sources.quote: START natural language system that allows the user to access various types of information using English

note: START (1993) answered open-ended English questions about places, people, movies and more over the Web, an earlier broad-domain system than Watson 2011; its knowledge came from hand-annotated sources so breadth is limited (hence low). what: First practical optical holograms recording 3D objects made by Denisyuk (USSR) and by Leith and Upatnieks (Michigan), viewable from several angles

what: Lloyd Cross produced a hologram recreating a moving 3-dimensional image (Multiplex hologram, viewable around a cylinder)

what: Manchester Baby (SSEM) had an output CRT displaying the bit pattern of its stores, from which results were read (working June 1948)

sources.title: Manchester Baby

what: Whirlwind became operational in 1951, real-time output on CRT displays used in Cape Cod radar tracking

sources.title: Whirlwind I

what: Takeo Kanade publicly demonstrated a face-matching system that located facial features and measured ratios without human intervention.

sources.title: Facial recognition system
sources.quote: In 1970, Takeo Kanade publicly demonstrated a face-matching system that located anatomical features such as the chin

note: Bledsoe, Chan and Bisson (1964-65) needed a human to mark feature coordinates, so rejected as semi-automated; the earlier system did the matching by computer, so a looser reading would date the demonstration to 1964-65.

what: The Bochum face-recognition system, by 1997 outperforming other systems, was sold commercially as ZN-Face to operators of airports and other busy locations.

sources.title: Facial recognition system
sources.quote: was sold commercially on the market as ZN-Face to operators of airports and other busy locations.

note: Earlier than Mexico 2000. The same article says West Virginia and New Mexico DMVs were first to use automated face recognition after 1993 (search results say West Virginia from 1998), but no dated source was fetchable. 1997 comes from ZN-Face commercial sale to airports, so it is a rough date.

what: Apple announced Face ID on the iPhone X, bringing face recognition to ordinary phone unlocking.

sources.title: Face ID
sources.quote: Apple announced Face ID alongside the iPhone X on September 12, 2017

note: Introduction date, not a measured adoption figure.
check_note: Introduction date, not a measured adoption figure. Earlier face-unlock phones (e.g. Android 4.0 Face Unlock, 2011) were niche and unreliable. Kept.

what: Herman Hollerith's electromechanical punched-card tabulator was used to process the 1890 US census.

sources.title: Unit record equipment
sources.quote: Hollerith's method was used in the 1890 census.

sources.title: Unit record equipment
sources.quote: The tabulator used electromechanical relays to increment mechanical counters.

note: The definition says 'computers and machines' doing clerical work, so machines count. Hollerith's tabulator is the earliest machine for mass clerical record processing; payroll and accounting uses of unit-record equipment followed. This is a judgement call: the census is government record processing, not an office as such. LEO I (1951) was the first business computer application but is later.

what: LEO I did real clerical work for Lyons (bakery valuations, later payroll and invoicing).

sources.title: LEO (computer)
sources.quote: LEO I ran its first business application in 1951.

sources.title: LEO (computer)
sources.quote: Lyons used LEO I initially for valuation jobs, but its role was extended to include payroll, inventory, and so on.

note: Same event as the demonstration, in service for Lyons's own business.
check_note: Looked for earlier clerical machines: Hollerith/Powers punched-card tabulators did accounting from the 1890s-1900s, but no fetched page gave a dated billing or payroll use, and the concept is computer-based office automation (term from the 1970s). LEO I is the first computer doing routine clerical work.

what: Westinghouse engineer Jim Sutherland's home-built ECHO IV computer, running household functions in his house, was made public.

sources.title: ECHO IV
sources.quote: It was made public for the first time in 1966.

note: Considered earlier appliance automation (1900s electric appliances, Monsanto House of the Future 1957) but those were not machines responding to occupants under computer control. ECHO IV is the earliest house run by a computer found; the exact 1966 date (April per CHM) rests on a secondary source and the CHM page could not be fetched.

what: ECHO IV served the Sutherland household's daily routines in his home through 1976.

sources.title: ECHO IV
sources.quote: The computer was working in the Sutherland's house until 1976, and was donated to the Computer Museum in Boston in 1984.

note: Same event as the demonstration; it was a one-off home-built prototype in real daily use for about a decade. No earlier real-household use found.

what: Stanley Works engineers Raymond and Roby designed an optical-sensor device that opened a door automatically; installed at Wilcox's Pier Restaurant, West Haven, CT.

sources.title: Automatic door
sources.quote: In 1931, engineers Horace H. Raymond and Sheldon S. Roby of the tool and hardware manufacturer Stanley Works designed the first model of an optical

note: Heron of Alexandria's temple doors (1st c. AD) were opened by fire-driven water pressure, not by a sensor detecting a person, so rejected. No contemporary 1931 report could be retrieved; only encyclopedic sources agree.

what: The Stanley optical door was installed in a West Haven, Connecticut restaurant for waiters carrying food.

sources.title: Automatic door
sources.quote: installed in Wilcox's Pier Restaurant in West Haven, Connecticut for the benefit of waiters carrying plates of food and drink

note: Installed and sold for $100, so a real use outside the lab. The first-pass 1960 Horton date is the first commercial sliding door, later than this.

what: Microwave motion detectors made sensor doors common in the 1970s.

sources.title: Automatic door
sources.quote: microwave motion detectors became common in automatic doors in the 1970s

note: Wikipedia only says detectors became common in doors then; exact year of routine public use not established (Horton commercial sliding doors from 1960 were mat-actuated).

what: ENIAC produced the first computer weather forecasts (Charney, Fjortoft, von Neumann).

sources.title: Numerical weather prediction
sources.quote: The ENIAC was used to create the first weather forecasts via computer in 1950

note: Richardson's 1922 hand-computed forecast was not computer-run and failed, so rejected. Automatic weather stations (e.g. a Friez/Bendix unit reportedly finished spring 1941, delivered to the US Navy 1942, per a 1947 USNI article that could not be fetched) are an earlier sensor-only candidate that I could not verify with a quote.

what: Rossby's group at the Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute produced the first routine operational computer forecast.

sources.title: Numerical weather prediction
sources.quote: In 1954, Carl-Gustav Rossby's group at the Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute used the same model to produce the first operational forecast

note: Earlier than the first-pass JNWPU May 1955 (which Wikipedia gives as the US start). Possible earlier operational automatic weather stations (1941-42) unverified.

what: Sidney Pressey at Ohio State built a mechanical machine that presented multiple-choice questions and scored answers without a teacher.

sources.title: Intelligent tutoring system
sources.quote: date back as early as 1924, when Sidney Pressey of Ohio State University created a mechanical teaching machine to instruct students without a human teacher

sources.title: teaching machine
sources.quote: inception (P571): 1920s

note: Dates differ across sources (1924 vs mid-1920s, one says 1926). Earlier mechanical test-scorers not found. It is mechanical, not a computer, but fits the definition (presents questions, grades answers).

what: PLATO I began operating on the University of Illinois ILLIAC I computer as the first generalized computer-assisted instruction system.

sources.title: PLATO (computer system)
sources.quote: Starting in 1960, it ran on the University of Illinois's ILLIAC I computer.

note: Pressey's machine saw only limited classroom/commercial use (Welch contract failed ~1929, not verified by a fetched quote). PLATO I was largely an experiment, so practical use is uncertain.

what: MYCIN, a Stanford expert system for diagnosing infections, was developed from early in the 1970s.

sources.title: MYCIN
sources.quote: MYCIN was developed over five or six years in the early 1970s at Stanford University.

note: Earlier candidates: Ledley and Lusted 1959 (Science) was a theoretical argument not a working system (Wikipedia Ledley article); Warner's 1961 Bayesian heart disease program and de Dombal's Leeds abdominal pain system (1971-72) are probably earlier or comparable working systems but I could not fetch a source with a quote. Date is approximate.

what: Weizenbaum's ELIZA/DOCTOR script, a computer program imitating a Rogerian psychotherapist, was published in 1966.

sources.title: ELIZA
sources.quote: In Weizenbaum's 1966 article, he described ELIZA as a system that applied a pattern-matching mechanism along with interchanging scripts

note: Pattern matching only; it does not assess personality or deliver real therapy. Colby, Watt and Gilbert published 'A computer method of psychotherapy' in 1966 (PubMed 5936301, not fetched) which is of similar date. PARRY (1972) simulates a patient not a therapist.

what: Cesare Lombroso used a device measuring blood pressure changes on criminal suspects in police cases.

sources.title: Polygraph
sources.quote: Early devices for lie detection include an 1895 invention of Cesare Lombroso used to measure changes in blood pressure for police cases

note: Earlier than Larson's 1921 polygraph. Lombroso measured blood pressure/pulse only, not breathing or skin conductance, so fit is partial; Benussi 1904 (breathing) and Mackenzie 1906 also precede Larson. Dating of Lombroso is secondary-source only.

what: Larson's polygraph, recording blood pressure and breathing, was first applied in law enforcement by the Berkeley Police Department.

sources.title: Polygraph
sources.quote: first applied in law enforcement work by the Berkeley Police Department under its nationally renowned police chief August Vollmer

note: Lombroso's 1895 police use may be earlier but is a less certain, single-signal device; Larson's multi-signal instrument is the first to match the definition and be routinely applied.

what: Hans Berger recorded the first human EEG in Jena.

sources.title: Electroencephalography
sources.quote: German physiologist and psychiatrist Hans Berger (1873–1941) recorded the first human EEG in 1924.

note: Caton recorded animal brain electricity in 1875 but not humans, so rejected. Berger published in 1929.

what: Gibbs, Davis and Lennox described EEG spike-wave patterns of epilepsy, starting clinical electroencephalography; first EEG lab opened at Massachusetts General Hospital in 1936.

sources.title: Electroencephalography
sources.quote: Gibbs, Davis and Lennox described interictal spike waves and the three cycles/s pattern of clinical absence seizures, which began the field of clinical electroencephalography.

note: Fisher and Lowenbach demonstrated epileptiform spikes in 1934; that is a research finding, not clinical service, so 1935 chosen. Berger himself used EEG on patients from 1920s but no clinical service is documented.

what: ATR labs in Kyoto reconstructed 10x10-pixel images a person viewed from brain signals.

sources.title: Brain-computer interface
sources.quote: allowed researchers to reconstruct images from brain signals at a resolution of 10×10 pixels

note: Only seen images are decoded, not specific thoughts or memories, so it is a partial fit; Nishimoto 2011 movie reconstruction is later. Yang Dan 1999 decoded images from cat thalamus (animal, rejected).
check_note: Earlier decoding of seen orientations (Kamitani and Tong 2005) decodes simple features, not images; Yang Dan 1999 cat thalamus is animal. Partial fit (seen images, not thoughts), but nothing earlier fits better.

what: Chang and Makin at UCSF decoded spoken sentences from ECoG signals into text with 3% word error rate.

sources.title: Brain-computer interface
sources.quote: Edward Chang and Joseph Makin from UCSF reported that ECoG signals could be used to decode speech from epilepsy patients

note: Decodes overt speech from a 50-sentence set, not private thoughts; Willett et al. 2021 (attempted handwriting to text) is later and could not be quoted. P300 speller (1988) selects letters by attention, not thoughts. Poor fit overall.
check_note: Earlier brain-to-letter systems (P300 speller 1988, Birbaumer slow-cortical-potential spelling 1999) select letters by attention or self-regulation, not by decoding thoughts, so rejected. Poor fit overall but the earliest brain-to-text decoding of language found.

what: Alvin Lucier's Music for Solo Performer (1965) used a performer's EEG alpha waves, via amplifiers and filters, to drive percussion instruments.

sources.title: Brain-computer interface
sources.quote: one of the earliest examples of a working brain–machine interface was the piece Music for Solo Performer (1965) by American composer Alvin Lucier.

note: Wikipedia calls it a working brain-machine interface 12 years before Vidal's 1977 EEG cursor/maze demonstration (the original). It is an art piece, so the fit is arguable; Fetz 1969 monkeys and Grey Walter 1964 rejected (animal / unverified).

what: Kennedy and Bakay implanted a locked-in patient, Johnny Ray, who learned to control a computer cursor.

sources.title: Brain-computer interface
sources.quote: Ray's implant was installed in 1998 and he lived long enough to start working with the implant, eventually learning to control a computer cursor

note: Birbaumer's slow cortical potential spelling device for paralysed patients (1999) is nearly contemporary; earlier lab cursor control with EEG (Wolpaw 1991) was not a service for patients.
check_note: Birbaumer's mid-1990s paralysed-patient cursor training was a lab experiment, and his spelling device is 1999; Dobelle's 1978 implant fed vision into the brain (machine to brain) and was a prototype; Dobelle's paid service is 2002. Nothing earlier found.

what: Djourno and Eyries in France invented the original cochlear implant, stimulating the auditory nerve electrically.

sources.title: Cochlear implant
sources.quote: André Djourno and Charles Eyriès invented the original cochlear implant in 1957.

note: Earlier than the first-pass House 1961. Cardiac pacemaker implants (1958) are body implants not neural/sensory, so rejected for this concept.

what: Hochmair's multichannel cochlear implant was first implanted in a person in Vienna, followed by Clark's in 1978; both were commercialized.

sources.title: Cochlear implant
sources.quote: with the Hochmairs' device first implanted in a person in December 1977 and Clark's in August 1978

note: House/3M single-channel devices were marketed from 1972 and FDA-approved for adults in 1984 (not verified with a fetched quote), which may be earlier practical use. Date here is a weak proxy.

what: Ivan Sutherland and students built a computer-driven head-mounted display (Sword of Damocles) at Harvard

sources.title: The Sword of Damocles (virtual reality)
sources.quote: The system was created in 1968 by computer scientist Ivan Sutherland with the help of his students Bob Sproull

note: Heilig's Sensorama (1962) rejected: mechanical, not computer-generated. Philco Headsight (1961) is camera-based, not a generated world. Primitive wireframe, so fit is partial.

what: Virtuality 1000SU VR systems launched in London in 1990 and sold to corporations (Ford, IBM, Mitsubishi, Olin) before the 1991 arcade version.

sources.title: Virtuality (product)
sources.quote: The Virtuality 1000SU VR system was launched in 1990 at the Computer Graphics ’90 exhibition held at Alexandra Palace in London.

sources.title: Virtuality (product)
sources.quote: Many other systems were sold to corporations including Ford, IBM, Mitsubishi and Olin.

note: Original 1991 arcade release was preceded by the 1990 corporate-sale product. Military helmet simulators and VPL's 1980s RB2 could be earlier but no fetched page dated a real-purpose use, so not adopted.

what: MUD (MUD1) created by Roy Trubshaw and Richard Bartle at Essex University, a multi-user shared text world

sources.title: MUD1
sources.quote: MUD was created in 1977 by Roy Trubshaw and Richard Bartle at the University of Essex on a DEC PDP-10.

note: Earlier: Maze War (two networked computers, 1973) and PLATO games like Empire (1973) are multi-user but game arenas rather than a world to meet in; considered and rejected, though arguable. First pass chose Habitat 1986 (graphical), later than MUD.

what: MUD1 opened over the Internet to outside players, the first Internet multiplayer online RPG

sources.title: MUD1
sources.quote: That same year, MUD1 became the first Internet multiplayer online role-play

note: Public remote play grew from 1983; Habitat (1986 beta, Club Caribe 1988) is later.

what: World of Warcraft passed 10 million subscribers

sources.title: World of Warcraft
sources.quote: On January 22, 2008, World of Warcraft had more than 10 million subscribers worldwide

note: Year is a judgment; online worlds were popular from about 2004-2005, but routine use by ordinary people is arguable.
check_note: Lineage (Korea) reported over 3 million subscribers at one point but no date could be verified; EverQuest (259k, 2000) and Ultima Online (250k peak, 2003) are far smaller. WoW's 2004 launch and 2005-06 sales suggest mass use began earlier, but 2008 is the only dated figure verified.

what: French military built the Antoinette barrel, a ground trainer for aircraft pilots

sources.title: Flight simulator
sources.quote: In 1910, on the initiative of the French commanders Clolus and Laffont and Lieutenant Clavenad, the first ground training aircraft for military aircraft were built.

note: Earlier than first pass (Link 1929). Antoinette barrel was a crude manually moved mock-up with controls; fit to instruments/motion is loose, hence low. Link Trainer (1929) is the first instrumented, pneumatically moved device; no earlier fully fitting one found.

what: Antoinette barrel used for military ground training of pilots in France

sources.title: Flight simulator
sources.quote: In 1910, on the initiative of the French commanders Clolus and Laffont and Lieutenant Clavenad, the first ground training aircraft for military aircraft were built.

note: Same event as demonstration; the source says it was built for military training. Link Trainer's 1934 USAAF purchase is later, so rejected as earliest.

what: Link Trainers mass-produced and used to train most Allied pilots in WWII

sources.title: Flight simulator
sources.quote: Some 10,000 were produced to train 500,000 new pilots from allied nations

sources.title: Flight simulator
sources.quote: The best-known early flight simulation device was the Link Trainer, produced by Edwin Link in Binghamton, New York

note: Year is approximate (wartime training 1941-45). Training of ordinary recruits, not consumers; consumer sims came later (1980s) and are not earlier.
